findings.claim: The native encoder constructs final v7 bytes in reusable parser memory, then JavaScript copies them to an owned Uint8Array. It does not currently compute the final base/derived envelope checksum. Reusing the existing XXH32 implementation would add final-byte scans in that worker while removing corresponding coordinator scans. It is work placement and possible implementation-speed change, not an already-proven eliminated pass.

Derived counts/postings are backfilled and rewritten during construction. Folding the exact final-order XXH32 stream into those writes is not the narrow post-encoder proposal and would need a separate algorithm proof. Existing key/content hashes cover different bytes and cannot substitute for the persisted base/derived checksums.

The segmented native plan intentionally aliases string bytes, key lengths and expression IDs into the owned v7 payload. Whole-group native indexes have a separately copied stable plan at baseline, but their prepared bytes remain exposed and mutable. Owned means independent of subsequent parser heap reuse; it does not mean immutable to every receiver/callback.

The existing worker transfer detaches the sender buffer but preserves all receiver-side aliases. The parser invokes/awaits its onChunk callback, and the receiver/database retain the prepared map across asynchronous deduplication/content persistence and record append steps. There is no existing lookup checksum witness or lookup-specific immutable-byte ownership contract.

The current final envelope operation validates fields/framing, hashes the bytes currently supplied, and copies those same bytes synchronously into an independent owned envelope. The earlier _encodeArtifactChunkRecords and _validateShardAppendFormat awaits separate this operation from native production. Replacing current-byte hashing by a producer value would allow an unchanged object identity/descriptor with altered bytes to carry a stale checksum. A WeakMap, map entry or descriptor/length check alone cannot prove byte immutability.

The later loader recomputes base/derived/record-field checksums. A stale producer value can therefore cause a persisted import to fail readback, or invoke derived repair, instead of describing the current snapshot as baseline does. Preserving validation requires proven exclusive immutable ownership through the final snapshot or revalidation of the actual bytes; the latter restores the checksum scan.

Whole/segmented preparation, missing/incomplete maps and content-offset-driven splits have fallback behavior. A checksum protocol would need exact byte-range and format identity, transfer/detachment failure handling, and ordinary fallback for all these cases. No safe narrow fast path satisfying the requested unchanged mutable-byte contract was established.

Even a safe producer checksum would leave record-field encoding/hash, score-key and framing validation, final envelope allocation/copies, and persistence unchanged. Those fields depend on sink-selected content offsets and are not present in the parser-side lookup container.

PR #820 current f65f4ef uses producer/descriptor geometry for buffer reuse and explicitly keeps in-place edits visible to existing validation; it is not an immutable checksum witness. PR #877 atomically transfers eligible owned envelope parts before asynchronous I/O-worker hashing; it does not reuse an earlier checksum, keeps alias fallbacks, and its existing source-size eligibility excludes the ordinary JMdict path. PR #977 changes content preparation/metadata/completion ownership and scheduling, not lookup payload immutability or final lookup checksums.

requirementsBeforeAnyFuturePrototype: Establish an exact internal producer-to-final-snapshot byte-ownership contract rather than trusting mutable descriptors or an enumerable checksum field.
Preserve existing caller mutation/alias/fallback behavior, including whole and segmented plans and content-offset splits.
Show where native final-byte hashing runs and whether it extends the critical worker straggler; byte volume alone is not a latency estimate.
Check compatibility with concurrent #820 and #977 before changing ownership or lifetime semantics.
